title: Causal Preference Elicitation
claim: Our query-selection strategy concentrates the posterior faster and recovers the true structure better than baselines under a limited query budget.
layout: 3 line-plot panels in a row, shared x-axis, shaded variance bands
description: A single row of three line plots, all plotted against query Round (0 to about 190). The left panel shows predictive entropy, the middle panel shows structural Hamming distance (SHD), and the right panel shows expected true class probability (ETCP). Each panel has four colored curves with shaded bands for one standard deviation: CaPE in dark blue, UNC in orange, RND in gray, and STE in light blue. All curves start from the same point. The proposed CaPE curve drops fastest and reaches the lowest entropy and SHD. In the right panel it climbs to the highest ETCP, near 1.0. The gray random baseline is clearly the slowest. The orange UNC curve plateaus early with a wide band. The legend sits inside each panel.
caption: Synthetic-data results comparing expert query strategies. Average predictive entropy (Entropy ↓), structural Hamming distance (SHD ↓) to the ground-truth graph, and expected true class probability (ETCP ↑). The means ± one standard deviations (as shaded areas) across 10 replications are reported.
abstract: We propose causal preference elicitation, a Bayesian framework for expert-in-the-loop causal discovery that actively queries local edge relations to concentrate a posterior over directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). From any black-box observational posterior, we model noisy expert judgments with a three-way likelihood over edge existence and direction. Posterior inference uses a flexible particle approximation, and queries are selected by an efficient expected information gain criterion on the expert's categorical response. Experiments on synthetic graphs, protein signaling data, and a human gene perturbation benchmark show faster posterior concentration and improved recovery of directed effects under tight query budgets.
